title: Invitation, not instruction
hookLine: Arjuna's bow slips from his hands; after the whole Gita, Krishna says: reflect, then do as you choose
tomorrow: what did a man say when he woke up on a stone pillow?

lines: COME IF YOU LIKE, OR DO IT.
THE BOW SLIPS FROM HIS HANDS.
cards: Two notes on the fridge. One says: pizza night, come if you like. The other says: take out the trash.
Same kitchen, a different weight in your hands. The Bhagavad Gita opens with sound: conch shells blown across a battlefield, Krishna's among them. Then a weight.

The warrior Arjuna looks across at the other army, sees his own teachers and cousins, and his bow slips from his hands. He sinks down in his chariot. His charioteer is Krishna, who in the Gita is God.
What follows is the whole teaching. But listen for how it ends.

teach.b: Krishna teaches chapter after chapter: on duty, on the self that doesn't die, on acting without clinging to results, on devotion. He even shows Arjuna his cosmic form.
And then, near the end, after all of it, God says something surprising. I have told you this wisdom.

teach.h: REFLECT, THEN DO AS YOU CHOOSE.
teach.b: Reflect on it fully, and then do as you choose. In Sanskrit, yathecchasi tatha kuru. Not obey.
Not because I said so. In this scripture, God hands the choice back. And Arjuna answers that his confusion is gone and he will do as Krishna says.
The bow he let fall in the first chapter is his to take up again, by his own yes. He speaks once more after that, a last word of love and refuge, but the choice has already been handed back.
Here the teaching is offered in full, reflected on, then chosen. A practice that's forced stays the teacher's.
A practice that's chosen becomes yours.
So an invitation isn't a weaker kind of instruction. In this verse of the Gita, it's how God offers the whole teaching.
Which matters when you're the one passing a practice on: offer it whole, warmly, and leave the hands free to pick it up.

how: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita, whose teaching ends with Krishna telling Arjuna to reflect fully and then choose; people who borrow it offer a practice and leave the choice free.

o: a printed card asking you to a big party
a polite way of giving someone an order
something offered warmly, free to take up

games.q: the end of the Gita: tap the pairs.
p: slips from his hands before the teaching
teaches it all, then hands back the choice

s: the Gita ends with Krishna simply ordering Arjuna to fight
near the end he says: reflect on it fully, then do as you choose, and Arjuna answers for himself.
Arjuna's bow slips from his hands before the teaching begins
he sinks down in his chariot, unwilling to fight his own teachers and cousins.

games.q: your partner wants you both to start meditating and has already booked you into a 6 a.m. class. you're annoyed. what fits Gita 18.63?
o: ask him to offer it, say why it matters, and let you decide.
go anyway; a good practice is worth it even when it's imposed.
refuse outright; anything someone else suggests isn't yours.
games.why: Krishna taught at length, then said: reflect on it fully, and do as you choose. Arjuna's yes was his own.

practice: Pick up something with a little weight: a book, a mug, your phone. Feel it in your hands, then set it down and let your hands rest open for a few breaths.
When you're ready, pick it up again, slowly, because you choose to, and notice how the same weight feels when it's yours.

wordCard.voice: Invitation: a practice offered whole and warmly, with the choice left in the other person's hands, the way the Gita ends.

orig.note: Sanskrit: do as you choose, Krishna's words to Arjuna near the end of the Bhagavad Gita (18.63).

carryVoice: Here's the line: an invitation, offered whole, the choice left free, the way Arjuna's yes was his own. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.12-19 (the conches), 1.29-30 (the bow Gandiva slips from his hand), 1.47 (Arjuna sinks down, casting away bow and arrows)
Bhagavad Gita 18.63 (reflect on this fully, then do as you wish) and 18.73 (Arjuna: my delusion is gone; I will do your word)
